# EC601 Design Proposal

## Elena Berrios, Sean O’Connor

# SCOS Device for Measuring Blood Flow

## Background

Most wearable heart-rate sensors, including smartwatches and pulse oximeters, rely on a technique called photoplethysmography (PPG), which shines light into the skin and measures how much bounces back as blood volume rises and falls with each heartbeat. PPG is useful, but it only reveals how much blood is present at a given moment, not how fast it's moving- and that flow information turns out to matter for estimating blood pressure without a cuff. Speckle Contrast Optical Spectroscopy (SCOS) is a newer optical technique that fills this gap: it uses coherent laser light, which forms a fine, grainy interference pattern (called speckle) on a camera sensor, and the way that pattern blurs from one moment to the next reveals how fast blood cells are moving beneath the skin. Recent biomedical research has shown that combining this flow information with traditional PPG volume data meaningfully improves cuffless blood pressure accuracy compared to PPG alone. This project builds a low-cost, DIY version of a SCOS sensor to explore that same underlying principle- using affordable, hobbyist-grade hardware to demonstrate that the physics behind this cutting-edge research technique can be observed and validated on a modest budget.

*Example SCOS setup. The laser diode emits light at an angle into arm tissue, and the camera measures the speckle pattern from scattered light. A basic 3D-printed mount holds the laser and camera in place.*

## Mission and Primary User

For students exploring optical blood-flow sensing with limited equipment, this project provides a low-cost experimental setup and documented analysis to determine whether a Raspberry Pi, camera, and small laser can produce useful speckle measurements. Unlike purchasing a research instrument, this approach evaluates what can be achieved with hardware students already own.

The primary users are our project team and other students who may reproduce or extend the experiments.

## Assumptions to Validate

| Assumption | Initial test | Decision if unsupported |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Our camera and laser can resolve speckle. | Capture a stationary scattering target across a documented range of focus, aperture, and exposure settings. | Identify whether optics, illumination, or camera limitations prevent further measurement. |
| Contrast changes are distinguishable from noise. | Repeat stationary and controlled-motion trials while recording intensity and camera settings. | Focus the project on characterizing the limiting noise or instability. |
| A simple printed jig can provide consistent geometry. | Compare measurements across repeated placements. | Revise the jig or limit conclusions to a fixed benchtop setup. |
| Skin measurements contain information beyond contact and motion artifacts. | If appropriate for the selected laser and campus requirements, compare repeated stationary recordings with deliberate repositioning controls. | Report the ambiguity without claiming blood-flow measurement. |

## User Stories and Acceptance Criteria

| User story | Acceptance criteria |
| :---- | :---- |
| As a student experimenter, I want to capture images with known settings so that I can compare trials fairly. | Save raw images with timestamps, exposure, and gain; keep settings fixed within each comparison. |
| As a student experimenter, I want to inspect speckle contrast so that I can determine whether the setup produces a measurable signal. | Calculate and plot contrast and mean intensity for a defined image region; retain the source images. |
| As a student experimenter, I want to compare stationary and moving conditions so that I can assess sensitivity to motion. | Complete at least five repeated comparisons under documented conditions and report the effect alongside baseline variability. |
| As a student experimenter, I want a repeatable mounting arrangement so that placement changes do not dominate the results. | Produce a jig design and quantify measurement variation across repeated placements. |
| As another student, I want the methods and results documented so that I can reproduce the experiment and judge its limitations. | Provide the component list, setup geometry, software, example data, and a conclusion tied to measured evidence. |

## Decision Criteria and Definition of Success

We will test the most consequential uncertainty first: whether the available camera and inexpensive laser can resolve usable speckle.

If documented adjustments cannot produce a resolvable pattern, we will stop progressing toward skin measurements and investigate the limiting factors. If contrast changes remain indistinguishable from noise or artifacts, we will report that limitation rather than interpret them as blood flow.

The project succeeds by producing reproducible experiments and an evidence-based conclusion about feasibility with our selected hardware. A negative or inconclusive result is valuable when it establishes what was tested, what limited the measurements, and what would be required to proceed. A complete integrated device is a stretch goal.
